mappings.note: Asks the learner to speak about their own experience of sending a money order; it never returns to the story, so it is personal expression, not a literature outcome under C-E1.4.
Sentence-joining drill with the relative pronoun cue '(whom)'. Pure grammatical convention, so C-E1.3 rather than the comprehension competency C-E1.1.
A sentence-completion/combining exercise using a line from the story as raw material; the skill tested is sentence structure, not understanding of the text.
Find metaphors in the story and say what quality is transferred. Figurative language is a literary convention and none of the three LOs names it, so the competency is the most specific legal code.
Straight retrieval of a fact stated in the prose (Lencho hoped for rain). Not LO-2, because no judgement about character is required.
Requires interpreting the image 'new coins' - why the writer/Lencho uses it. Inferring and interpreting sits with C-E1.1; it is not a theme question (LO-1) nor a character one (LO-2).
Two facts to extract from the narrative (rain turned to hail; the field was ruined). Information retrieval, so LO-1, not the character outcome LO-2.
Asks about Lencho's state of mind after the hail - his despair and sense of total loss. That is character and context analysis (LO-2), not plain fact retrieval (LO-1).
Lencho's faith is the defining trait of the character, and the question pairs it with the action it produced. LO-2 rather than LO-1 because it is about who he is, not what the text says happened.
Single-fact retrieval (the postmaster read the letter). No analysis of the postmaster is asked for, so not LO-2.
Next-event question in the oral comprehension check; the expected answer is the sequence of actions, so LO-1 rather than the motive question that would make it LO-2.
Lencho's lack of surprise only makes sense as a statement about his character, so LO-2. LO-1 would apply if the answer were a plot event rather than a disposition.
Explains Lencho's anger at receiving 70 of the 100 pesos - motive and mindset, i.e. character in context (LO-2), not a retrievable fact (LO-1).
Explicitly demands the sentences from the story that prove the claim. LO-3 is the outcome that names textual evidence; LO-2 would cover the character half alone.
Both halves probe the postmaster's motive for the deception - character and the writer's point about kindness. Not LO-1, which would only need the event.
The 'why/why not' turns a yes/no fact into an account of Lencho's simplicity and faith, so character analysis (LO-2) rather than retrieval (LO-1).
The question defines and then applies situational irony - a literary convention. None of the three LOs names figures or devices, so the competency C-E1.4 is the most specific honest code.
First half asks the learner to judge whether such people exist in the real world (opinion, C-E1.2); second half is a character verdict on Lencho (LO-2). Not LO-1, since nothing is retrieved.
Man-versus-nature and man-versus-man are the story's two sub-themes; LO-1 is the outcome that names sub-themes. LO-2 would fit only if the focus were a single character.
Word-building puzzle for storm vocabulary (cyclone, gale, typhoon). Vocabulary sits in C-E1.1; C-E1.3 covers grammar, which is not what is tested.
Matching a sentence to the meaning of an idiom ('wishing for something very unlikely') - word and phrase meaning, so C-E1.1 and not a literature outcome.
A form-filling and 'Space for Communication' writing task judged on correct format; C-E1.2 explicitly names format. Not C-E1.3, since no grammatical structure is being drilled.
Personal-response prompt about a difficulty of one's own; the answer never touches the text, so it belongs to expression of opinion and experience, not to C-E1.4.
Comprehension of the sample informal letter in the writing section, not of the story itself, so plain decoding/comprehension under C-E1.1 rather than a prose-extract outcome.
Setting detail stated in the first line of the story. Retrieval, so LO-1; nothing about the writer's message is asked.
Identifies the irony of the story in MCQ form - a literary convention, which only the C-E1.4 competency covers; LO-1 would misread it as a theme question.
Asks which conflicts the chapter highlights - the sub-themes named in LO-1. Not C-E1.4 generally, because the LO is the more specific fit.
MCQ retrieval of the same stated fact (rain for the crop). LO-1, not LO-2, because Lencho's character is not in question.
The reason for needing money (to keep the family from hunger) is stated in the letter; retrieval rather than inference about character.
Plot-event MCQ on what the postmaster did. Retrieval (LO-1); the motive version of this question is mapped to LO-2 elsewhere in this batch.
Tests recall of the writer's coin imagery for the raindrops - recognising the figure the author used, so the literary-conventions competency rather than LO-1 retrieval of plot.
'Frozen pearls' is the story's metaphor for hailstones; the item tests recognition of the figure, which no LO names, so C-E1.4.
Time detail (Sunday morning) taken straight from the prose. LO-1 retrieval.
Numerical detail from the text (70 pesos). Retrieval only, so LO-1 rather than the irony competency, even though the number is what triggers the irony.
Whom Lencho suspects is a statement about his distrust of people; that is character, so LO-2 rather than LO-1.
'A bunch of crooks' is Lencho's own judgement of the clerks - his attitude, hence LO-2. It is not a vocabulary item (C-E1.1); the word is given, not defined.
Requires matching the extract to the quote that captures its central idea (farming as a profession of hope) - theme identification, LO-1. Not LO-3, since no evidence has to be written out.
The postmaster's reason for signing as God is his motive - character and the writer's message about protecting faith, so LO-2.
The 'why not' answer is Lencho's complete faith: a trait, not an event, so LO-2 rather than LO-1.
What Lencho thinks happened to the money is his (mistaken) belief about people - character, LO-2. The factual answer would be the opposite of what he thinks.
